name: Block periodization

lead: Block periodization organises training into focused phases, each emphasising one quality, such as accumulating work, converting it to intensity, and then peaking. People use it to structure lifting so that progress continues over months, which supports building muscle and strength.
Research exists mainly in endurance athletes and in strength and power sports. A meta-analysis of endurance block training and several trials have been published, with results described below.

paras: Programs are divided into blocks lasting a few weeks, each with a dominant goal, followed by a change of focus. Lifters adjust volume, load and exercise selection between blocks and may include a lighter period before testing or competing.

Risks are those of any structured training: overuse injuries and fatigue if load increases too quickly. Reviews of related periodization models report that evidence for one model being superior is mixed.

angle.text: Block periodization changes how a lifter sequences work, aiming to keep progress moving across months. Appearance changes come from the muscle and strength built, with the block structure as the planning framework.

lead: Block periodization is a way of organising training into successive phases, called blocks, with each block concentrating most of its effort on a narrow set of goals rather than training every quality at once. It sits alongside traditional (linear), undulating and reverse periodization as one of the main models coaches use to plan a season or a training cycle.[1][2][3]

For appearance, the chain is planning to progression to muscle. A lifter who runs a block of higher-volume work and then a block of heavier, lower-volume work is trying to keep adding training capacity and strength, which is what ultimately lets a physique grow, building the shoulders, back, chest and legs. Block periodization is a way to sequence training, not a muscle-building stimulus in itself, and lifters on bodybuilding and strength forums describe sprinkling "hypertrophy blocks" between strength or strongman phases.[4]

The model is most closely associated with the Latvian-born sport scientist Vladimir Issurin, who in a 2010 Sports Medicine review argued that the traditional model, developed around five decades earlier, had limitations for high-level sport and proposed concentrated blocks as an alternative.[2] Published research includes a 2019 meta-analysis in endurance athletes, trials in cyclists, a 2023 randomised trial in resistance-trained men and a 2021 narrative review emphasising strength and power training.[5][6][7][8]

Endurance, strength, power and team-sport athletes

paras: In block periodization the training year, or a shorter cycle, is divided into blocks that each stress a limited number of abilities, rather than developing all qualities in parallel as in traditional models.[1][2] Issurin described the problems he saw in the traditional approach as conflicting physiological responses from mixed training aimed at many abilities, excessive fatigue from prolonged multi-targeted work, and insufficient stimulation from medium and low workloads for advanced athletes.[2]

Descriptions of the model commonly list three block types: an accumulation block that builds general work capacity and basic abilities, a transmutation (or transformation) block that converts that base into more specific, higher-intensity work, and a realization block that tapers load ahead of a test or competition. A 2021 narrative review by Stone and colleagues divides block periodization into single-goal and multiple-goal versions and concludes that appropriately programmed periodized training can outperform nonperiodized training, with each model having strengths and weaknesses that can be adapted to a sport.[7]
Block lengths in the research vary: a 2023 systematic review of trained cyclists found block periodization used blocks of one to eight weeks of high-, medium- or low-intensity training.[9]

Planned variation in training has a long history in sport science. Wikipedia's article on sports periodization credits Hans Selye's 1957 general adaptation syndrome as the physiological framework, the Soviet physiologist Leo Matveyev with a formalised model around 1964 drawn from analysis of Soviet athletes at the 1952 and 1956 Olympics, and the Romanian sport scientist Tudor Bompa with expanding it.[10] J. Garhammer published one of the first articles on periodizing strength training in 1979, and information about Soviet methods reached US strength coaches through Grigori Goldstein in 1988.[10]

In the traditional model, a macrocycle (often the full season) is divided into mesocycles of several weeks and microcycles of about a week, moving from a long general preparation phase through competition to a short transition period.[10] Block periodization departs from this by concentrating work on fewer targets at a time.[2]

Lifters on forums and in coaching literature use blocks to separate phases such as higher-volume muscle building and lower-volume, heavier strength work, sometimes adding a strongman or powerlifting emphasis for variety. One member of a T Nation training-log thread describes growing muscle as helpful for "pretty much anything" and says hypertrophy blocks were sprinkled in between other phases.[4]

A 2018 review of strength training considerations notes that single- and multi-targeted block models may produce the greatest strength and power benefits, while adding that concepts within each model must be considered within the limits of the sport, the athlete and the schedule.[1] Because strength is underpinned by muscle cross-sectional area, architecture and neural factors, the review is relevant to lifters whose goal is a larger, stronger physique.[1]

The strongest body of block periodization research is in endurance sport. A 2014 study in trained cyclists by Rønnestad, Hansen and Ellefsen compared a block of five high-intensity sessions in one week followed by three weeks of one weekly high-intensity session with a traditional distribution. Over four weeks the block group (10 cyclists) improved VO2max by 4.6 percent, maximal aerobic power by 2.1 percent and power at 2 mmol/L lactate by 10 percent, while the traditional group (9 cyclists) showed no significant changes; volumes were similar.[8]

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis by Mølmen, Øfsteng and Rønnestad screened 2,905 records, included 20 studies and pooled six. It found small effects favouring block periodization for VO2max (standardised mean difference 0.40) and maximal power output (0.28), with a mean methodological quality score of 3.7 out of 10, leading the authors to urge caution.[5] A 2023 systematic review of seven cyclist studies found improvements in aerobic measures under both block and traditional models and no evidence favouring either over eight to twelve weeks.[9] A 2025 randomised crossover trial in 30 well-trained cyclists reported improvements after a moderate-intensity interval block compared with regular training.[11]

A 2023 randomised trial by Bartolomei and colleagues assigned 22 resistance-trained men to a mixed-session program or a block-periodized program with equated volume for ten weeks. The mixed-session group gained more fat-free mass, pectoralis and vastus lateralis thickness and bench press strength (about 8.6 percent versus 2 percent), while the block group improved vertical jump more (about 7.2 percent versus 1.2 percent).[6]

In a 2017 study of six collegiate throwers on a 12-week block-periodized model ending in an overreach and taper, five of six improved throwing performance and countermovement jump force and power improved, while vastus lateralis thickness rose after the in-season phase but not after the taper.[12] A 14-day high-intensity shock microcycle trial in 14 ice hockey players found improvements in a repeated high-intensity running test relative to a control group.[13]

Reverse periodization, which sequences work in the opposite order from the traditional model, was examined in a 2022 systematic review of 11 studies and 200 athletes, which found it did not give superior improvements in swimming, running, muscular endurance, maximum strength or VO2max compared with traditional or block periodization.[3]

Wikipedia's sports periodization article records criticism that periodization models can be reductionist and may overlook individual hormonal, genetic, motivational and environmental differences, citing a 2017 review by Kiely in Sports Medicine that questioned traditional models.[10] Issurin himself framed block periodization as a response to contradictions between older models and the demands of high-performance sport.[2]

The research base is smaller in hypertrophy-focused lifters than in endurance athletes: the available resistance trials use short durations and small samples, and the cyclist meta-analysis reports low methodological quality scores.[5][6]

Human trials comparing block periodization with other organisations of training include the 2014 cyclist trial, the 2019 endurance meta-analysis, a 2023 systematic review in cyclists, a 2023 resistance-training randomised trial in 22 trained men, a 2025 crossover trial in 30 cyclists and small trials in throwers and hockey players.[5][6][9][8][11][12][13] The reverse periodization review found no superiority over traditional or block models across 11 studies.[3]

lore.intro: On lifting forums, blocks appear mainly as training-log vocabulary: members describe hypertrophy, strength or strongman blocks within longer logs.[4]

claims.claim: Alternating hypertrophy and strength blocks keeps muscle growth going
Reversing the order of phases (reverse periodization) is better

timeline.event: Hans Selye describes the general adaptation syndrome, later used as a framework for periodization.[10]
Leo Matveyev presents a formalised periodization model based on Soviet Olympic data.[10]
J. Garhammer publishes an early article on periodizing strength training.[10]
Grigori Goldstein shares Soviet periodization methods with US strength coaches.[10]
Issurin's Sports Medicine review proposes block periodization as an alternative to the traditional model.[2]
Trial in trained cyclists reports larger VO2max gains with a high-intensity block than traditional distribution.[8]
Study of collegiate throwers follows a 12-week block model with overreach and taper.[12]
Review of strength training considerations discusses block models for strength-power gains.[1]
First meta-analysis of block periodization in endurance athletes.[5]
Stone and colleagues publish a narrative review of periodization and block periodization for strength-power sport.[7]
Randomised trial compares mixed-session and block-periodized resistance programs in 22 trained men.[6]
